definitions.definition: A systematic VLSI design methodology covering specification, design entry, synthesis, verification, layout and fabrication, aimed at minimising design cycle time and maximising chip quality and reliability.
Design approach in which every transistor is individually drawn and all layers are customised; gives highest density and performance but is expensive with a long design time.
Design approach based on the standard cell methodology, in which cells designed and verified once for a given technology are reused many times across chip designs.
Collection of commonly used cells such as NANDs, NORs, AOIs, MUXes, adders and memory elements that are developed, characterised and stored once, then reused in many designs.
Array-based ASIC approach with pre-diffused base cells of fixed device size - channeled, channel-less (sea-of-gates) or structured/embedded - in which only the interconnect is customised.
The basic unit of description in Verilog HDL, describing the functionality or structure of a digital design through its I/O ports and internal structural or behavioural statements.
Net data type representing the physical connection between structural entities; it stores no value and continuously follows the value of its driving circuit.
Register data type that stores a value from one procedural assignment to the next; it can be assigned values only within initial or always blocks.
The four logic values of Verilog: 0 (logic zero or false), 1 (logic one or true), x (unknown logic value) and z (high impedance).
Standard gate set such as and, nand, or, nor and not, provided as part of the Verilog language for switch- and gate-level modelling.
A Verilog module used only for simulation and never synthesised; it instantiates the module under test and applies stimulus signals to verify its behaviour.
MOS technology in which n-channel MOSFETs are fabricated on a p-type substrate through epitaxy, oxidation, photolithography, etching, doping and metallisation.
Technology that fabricates both NMOS and PMOS transistors on the same silicon wafer, giving low power dissipation per gate, high component density and fast switching.
CMOS fabrication approach in which a deep p-well is implanted in an n-substrate, with the nMOS transistors formed inside this well.
CMOS fabrication approach in which a deep n-doped region is diffused into a p-substrate to host pMOS transistors, using around eight masks.
CMOS process using separate deep p-well and n-well diffusions in an epitaxial layer, so both device types can be optimised independently.
Technology combining BJTs and MOSFETs on one monolithic chip by extending CMOS processing with a few extra masks, used to speed up VLSI circuits driving large loads.
n+ layer diffused into the substrate before epitaxy that lowers collector resistance and minimises parasitic collector-to-substrate current in npn transistors.
Process of transforming an HDL design into a gate-level netlist under specified constraints, via translation, optimisation and technology mapping to a target library.
Dataflow modelling mechanism in which a value is assigned to a net using assign [delay] LHS_net = RHS_expression; such assignments execute concurrently and are order-independent.
MOS transistor behaviour in which gate-induced channel charge Qc is moved from drain to source by Vds, so Ids depends on both Vgs and Vds.
Minimum gate voltage needed to neutralise stored charges in the dielectric and invert the silicon beneath the gate, switching an enhancement-mode transistor on.
Increase in threshold voltage of a MOS transistor as its source-to-substrate bias VSB rises, caused by depletion of charge carriers from the channel.
Parameter indicating the frequency response of a MOS circuit, given by the transconductance-to-gate-capacitance ratio; fast circuits need the highest possible gm.
Hazardous CMOS condition in which the parasitic two-transistor structure forms a self-sustaining low-resistance path between VDD and VSS; it can occur when β1 × β2 > 1.
A MOS transistor used as a switch in series with lines carrying logic levels, like relay contacts, enabling compact switching-logic arrays.
Logic gate with a pull-down n-channel transistor and a pull-up transistor in series between VDD and ground, restoring levels.
An inverter with an NMOS pull-down and PMOS pull-up in series between VDD and VSS, giving restored logic levels and near-zero static power.
Operating region in which the channel pinches off near the drain, so Ids becomes independent of Vds and the device acts like a current source.
Verilog procedural construct that starts execution at time 0 and executes only once; typically used for stimulus and waveform generation in testbenches.
Verilog procedural construct that starts at time 0 and executes repeatedly in a loop; it must include some form of timing control to avoid endless zero-delay looping.
Verilog procedural assignment using '=' that completes execution before the next statement runs, so statements take effect one after another.
A Verilog procedural assignment using '<=' where the right-hand side is evaluated and the assignment is scheduled for the end of the current time step.
Combinational circuit that adds two input bits and a carry-in to produce a sum and carry-out.
Logic block that converts a 3-bit input code into one of eight mutually exclusive one-hot output lines.
Logic block that converts one of eight active input lines into a 3-bit binary output code.
A colour-coded cartoon of a layout capturing topology and layer information, showing components, vias and their relative placement.
Line drawn in a CMOS stick layout to separate p-transistors from n-transistors so p-diff never touches n-diff; it represents the p-well boundary.
Design rules expressed in a single parameter λ that set out mask dimensions in a process- and feature-size-independent way, valid over a range of λ values.
Shrinking transistor dimensions, interconnect and separations (typically 10–20% linearly) to get smaller, faster, lower-power chips; common models are constant-field and constant-voltage scaling.
Fabrication step in which silicon reacts with oxygen at 1000–1200 °C in ultra-clean furnaces; the dry form uses O2 gas and the wet form uses steam.
Process of transferring a mask pattern to a layer on the chip by spinning photoresist, exposing it to light, developing and then etching, similar to a printing process.
High-temperature fabrication step in which impurity atoms move from a high-concentration to a low-concentration region through the silicon crystal, setting the desired doping profile.
A fabrication step where dopant ions are accelerated and embedded in the crystal lattice, giving accurate reproducible doping.
Fabrication step of depositing metal, normally aluminium via sputtering, over the whole wafer and then selectively etching it to interconnect the circuit components.
Wafer-level electrical check in which needles contact each die's bonding pads and the whole die is exercised; failed dice are marked with ink.
Packaging step in which tested dice are connected to package pins with fine gold wires and sealed in plastic or epoxy under vacuum or an inert atmosphere.
An integrated capacitor formed from the gate-to-source capacitance of a MOSFET, whose value depends on gate area.
Near-ideal integrated capacitor formed between two polysilicon layers on thick field oxide, so parasitic effects are minimal but a second poly layer is required.
Integrated component formed by a reverse-biased semiconductor boundary whose depletion region acts as the dielectric; used as a varactor and works only under reverse bias.
Resistance of a square of thin uniform film, measured between opposite sides and expressed in ohms per square regardless of the square's size.
Time for a signal to reach its destination; for a logic gate, from the input crossing 50% of its level to the output crossing 50%.
Gate delay set by the time constant of the driver's equivalent resistance and the total load capacitance, growing as either increases.
Number of gate inputs driven by the output of one logic gate; each extra load adds capacitance that slows the output transition.
Chain of successively larger buffers used to drive a very large load, instead of wiring one gate to many inputs, to limit total delay.
Digital circuit element whose function is undefined at manufacture and is set by programming the connections between its internal gates.
Programmable logic device with a programmable AND plane and fixed OR plane that builds sum-of-products outputs, faster and cheaper than a fully programmable array.
Device equivalent to several programmable array logic blocks linked by programmable interconnections in one chip, suited to wide combinational logic.
Reprogrammable integrated circuit built from a grid of programmable logic blocks linked by configurable connections, usually loaded from SRAM at power-up.
Small programmable element inside a logic cell that implements a logic function of its inputs, typically four-input.
Basic building unit of a field-programmable array, holding a few logic cells that each combine a lookup table, full adder and flip-flop.
